## Work log

<!-- Chronological, written as you go. What was actually done, why, what it cost.
     Reference commits and link to plans and notes. Prose beats a checklist here —
     this is the part you will actually reread in three months. -->

- **Measured the problem before designing for it.** 19.31 MB raw / 4.42 MB gzipped, 68,704
  buildings, 317,927 footprint vertices at a mean of 4.63 each, ~997k triangles. All of the
  triangles are buildings: roads are already a canvas texture and water and green are a few
  hundred flat polygons. So there was only ever one thing to cut.
- **"For phones we can have a prerendered cityscape so it's just an image no?"** — asked
  mid-session, and the answer turned out to be better than a workaround. `Diorama.tsx` sets
  `enableRotate={false}` on an orthographic camera, so **zooming is exactly a 2D scale of the
  projected image and panning is exactly a 2D translation**. A pre-rendered cityscape is not a
  lossy stand-in for the geometry — it is the same picture, and only resolution degrades.

  Where it wins: at district fit the whole 47 km² is 1,076 × 621 px on a phone. Where it fails:
  at block fit the same extent needs 1.07 Gpx on a phone and 6.5 Gpx on the laptop — a tile
  pyramid, i.e. rebuilding a slippy map. So an image answers the district register completely and
  the block register not at all.
- **`docs/roadmap.md` had already rejected pre-rendered raster** under *Device reach*: it "needs
  hand-maintained hit regions, an image set per scenario and zoom level, and hotspot coordinates
  kept in sync by hand". That objection is about who maintains the image, not about whether it is
  correct — generated from the scene document, all three derive and cannot drift. The roadmap's
  own preferred alternative ("render the same scene document to SVG or Canvas 2D with a
  painter's-algorithm isometric projection") is exactly the generator that got built.
- **Chose the hybrid**: geometry where there is content, raster where there is context — the
  hero/stock distinction `Buildings.tsx` already draws, pushed one step further.
  `plans/2026-09-21_backdrop-lod.plan.md`.
- **`lod.ts`** — the partition, 23 tests. At 1,250 m: 7,588 buildings / 112k triangles stay
  geometry (budget is 100–150k), 61,116 / 885k go to the backdrop. The radius is a proxy and says
  so; the real rule is that heroes are always geometry at any distance, so item 5's content takes
  over from distance without a code change. One contract question surfaced in test: a building
  whose centroid sits exactly on the centre survived `radiusM: 0`, so a non-positive radius now
  means "no geometry" explicitly rather than "whatever happens to sit on the centre".
- **Two depth slices, not one plane.** The backdrop hangs on a plane normal to the view direction,
  and one plane behind the near geometry would hide the far buildings standing between the camera
  and Wat Ket. Measured: **17,560 of the 61,116 are in front**. Cheap to fix at generation time,
  ugly to retrofit after authoring.
- **`scripts/render-backdrop.ts`** — planned as Python beside `build-region.py`, moved to
  TypeScript once it was clear it needs `lod.ts`, `shading.ts` and `theme.ts`. Mirroring three
  engine modules in another language is precisely the drift everything else here is designed
  against. PNG written by hand for the reason `build-region.py` gives: an image library's output
  varies by version and would destroy byte-identity.

  Greyscale-8, so the byte `getImageData` hands back **is** the tone index — `theme.ts` keeps the
  palette, exactly as it keeps the hypsometric ramp for the relief field. The precedent is the
  16 Sep brand swap: a backdrop with colours baked in would have quietly kept the 1967 PROGRESS
  palette while every other surface moved.

  **61,116 buildings → 547 KB** (386 + 161), 4096 × 2360 px at 0.4163 px/m, 5.8 s, byte-identical
  on a re-run. Rendered both slices through the real palette and looked at them: the old city's
  moat grid, the Ping, temples in civic teal, and the near disc as a clean elliptical hole. The
  two slices tile along a horizontal cut, which is what a constant-depth cut projects to.
- **Sized the raster by VRAM rather than by disk.** 4,096 px looked like the obvious width — the
  PNG is only 386 KB — until the number that actually binds: the browser expands an 8-bit
  greyscale texture to RGBA on upload, so both slices cost **77 MB of video memory at 4,096 and
  19 MB at 2,048**. Looked at the 2,048 render through the real palette before committing to it;
  buildings, roof and wall tones and the disc edge all still read. The projector can have its own
  build via `--width` when there is a projector in the room to judge it on.
- **Closed the staleness hole, which was a real gap in the morning's reasoning.** Asked why the
  backdrop is not simply re-rendered on build. The answer is that "derived rather than authored"
  — the whole reply to the roadmap's objection — only stays true if something re-derives it, and
  a committed artefact goes stale the moment `npm run fetch:osm` rewrites the document. So the
  generator now fingerprints its inputs (every footprint, height, kind and id, the hero set, its
  own parameters) into the sidecar, and a test recomputes it from the committed document.
  Verified by nudging one building 20 cm and watching the suite fail with the message naming the
  fix. Build-time rendering would give the same guarantee; committing keeps the exhibition off
  the critical path of a build step, which is the reason the scene document is committed and the
  Overpass cache is not.
- **Stopped at the generator.** The runtime half — schema entry, `BackdropPlane.tsx`, the Diorama
  wiring, the viewer payload and the pan clamp — is specified in the plan and not yet built, so
  nothing in the viewer has changed today. Triangle count in the browser is still 997k; what
  exists is the artefact and the machinery that makes it, verified byte-identical, checked by eye,
  and guarded against going stale.
